prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B020 is the one candidate every member placed first, and the reasons hold up on the evidence. The chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through identification of the biologically active GLP-1 peptide, to long-acting agonists is clear and independently confirmed. Large randomized outcome trials show cardiovascular and renal benefit alongside glycemic and weight effects, and the field is mature. The discovery is original physiology that changed practice, not an incremental improvement. After reading colleagues' attribution arguments I am moving from my opening trio (Drucker, Holst, Knudsen) to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Holst covers physiology and secretion, Mojsov the identification and synthesis of the active peptide, and Drucker the receptor biology and translation. That is a discovery-centred prize with a defensible logic, and it avoids having to place a pharmaceutical development contribution beside academic discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list cannot hold everyone who mattered: Knudsen's work on long-acting analogues is arguably what made the physiology usable, and others such as Habener sit outside the supplied names. Excluding Knudsen could be read as rewarding the idea over the drug and as leaving out the step that created the clinical effect. Priority over identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is also not fully settled from the supplied text. I also doubt a single-achievement prize is the best use of the committee's range, since B045 and B040 are strong enough to deserve serious consideration in a shared prize, and the three-person limit prevents combining them with B020 without dropping a core GLP-1 name.

responses.point: Mojsov, Holst and Drucker are the most defensible trio. Knudsen's development of long-acting analogues is major but is left out only because of the three-person limit, and others such as Habener complicate allocation.
responses.response: I partly concede. My opening put Knudsen in and Mojsov out, and I now think the discovery-centred trio is easier to justify, because Mojsov's identification of the active peptide is what made the physiology tractable. I do not agree that Knudsen is left out only for space. The honest framing is that the prize recognizes how the biology was discovered, and that the engineering of long-acting analogues is a later stage. If the committee prefers to honour the drug, the trio changes, and I would want that choice stated openly rather than reached by default.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B040 second but proposes only June and Sadelain. He argues that Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is less decisive for the CAR contribution, and that Eshhar's omission limits any fair configuration.
responses.response: I agree on Eshhar. A prize for CAR-T that leaves out the originator of the chimeric receptor concept would be hard to defend, and I take that as the main reason I keep B040 only as an alternative and not as a second prize part. I disagree on Rosenberg. His adoptive cell transfer and gene-modified lymphocyte work is the conceptual precursor, and trimming him to make a pair fit does not resolve the Eshhar problem, it only moves it. The pair of June and Sadelain is cleaner, but I would still want the committee to confirm it can be defended before putting it forward.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response (B052) second, as a conceptually original and mechanistically complete pathway with a clean two-person attribution (Mori and Walter), and treats it as mature.
responses.response: I rank B052 low in my opening list (eighth) and I accept his case on originality and attribution, which is the cleanest on the shortlist. Where I differ is on the medical side: the claim that the pathway matters for diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer is plausible, but therapeutic translation is still modest and partly speculative. I do not think that rules it out, since the prize has honoured basic mechanism before. But it argues for B052 as a later or companion prize, not a rival to GLP-1 this year, and I would want a colleague to show disease-relevant evidence beyond ISRIB-type efforts.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius places TNF blockade (B034) third and calls it fully mature, arguably overdue, with a clean Feldmann and Maini pair and an exceptionally clear path from mechanism to patients.
responses.response: The attribution is clean and the patient impact is not in doubt, so this is a serious candidate that I did not rank at all, and I should say why. The concern is that anti-TNF therapy rests on antibody engineering and on TNF biology done by others outside the credited names, so it reads more as a translational proof of concept than as a discovery. If the committee treats proof that blocking a single cytokine treats disease as a discovery in its own right, B034 is stronger than I weighted it. I would like her view on whether the contribution is really more than clinical validation.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should honour GLP-1 discovery and physiology or also the pharmaceutical development, and so whether Knudsen belongs in the trio instead of Mojsov or Drucker.
How the priority dispute over identifying the active GLP-1 peptide, including Habener's role outside the credited names, should be weighed.
Whether B045 should be preferred over a single GLP-1 prize, given the six-name attribution problem and early clinical translation.
Whether the CAR-T attribution can be made fair without Eshhar, who is outside the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have co-authored with colleagues (Linnarsson, Frisén) and share the KI institutional setting, but none of the shortlisted candidates is a documented collaborator, mentor or KI colleague, so no recusal appears warranted.
